6.00 p.m. 
National Framework for Curriculum in Schools, 2000 which put a premium on 
indigenous tradition in Indian history id entified largely with the ancient Indian 
values. Later developments in Indian history are seen as irrelevant, if not 
harmful.' Sir, not a word has been stated  in the debate that preceded me to 
suggest that these conclusions ere eit her perverse or unsubstantiated. The 
distinguished former HRD Minister stated that he could find no basis for this 
conclusion, but, Sir, I only need to point the attention of this House to thirty 
pages given in Appendix-1 to thif report which have specifically and 
categorically delineated what the histor ians consider as 'aberrations' in the 
writing of history. Sir, in this factual background, the matter, by Public Interest 
Litigation was brought to the Supreme Court. A lot has been said as to the 
purport of this Supreme Court ju dgement, and, Sir, the Supreme Court 
judgment has been ad nauseam misquoted. In fact, Sir, Justice Sinha writing 
for the Supreme Court said that 'it is true that CABE, an institutional process to 
oversee everything about educational writing, was not consulted', and it was 
an institutional process in place from 1935 to 1994. 
For sixty long years, without a br eak, there has been a tradition, a 
custom, a convention, a practice, of ge tting the curricula vetted, scrutinized, 
approved, deliberated upon, by the Ge neral Committee of the NCERT, by its 
Executive Committee and then, by CABE. 
(MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair) 
None of these institutions were asked to deliberate, and suddenly, 
from nowhere, we find that there is a cu rriculum, which is inflicted on millions 
of students of History in this country. 
Sir, in a liberal tradition of this Republic, which finds mention and 
endorsement in as sacred a document as the Constitution of India, can we, in 
that context, not even take steps to rectify the aberrations? I ask myself this 
question, and I commend this question to the Members of this hon. House - if 
a particular aberration is specifically pointed out, is it not incumbent on the 
succeeding Government, which went to the polls on the plea of rectifying the 
aberrations of history, to correct the distortions of History? 
Sir, I lay no claim to an absolute standard of History; no one can. 
History is always in a state of evolution. History is evolved as societies 
311 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2004] 
evolve, as democracies mature. People give their own imprint to historical 
processes. Therefore, no one claims abso lutes in History. Bu t fidelity to facts 
from Karl Popper, to E.H. Kar, to Gibon, to Romila Thapar, to A. L. Bashum, to 
Nizami, to Irfan Habib, has been the tradition. Fidelity to facts is never 
compromised. 
Sir, my respectful submission for consideration of this House, on a 
matter of grave national importance is, have we prostituted facts, have we 
suborned facts of history, and have we de liberately done that? It is my guess, 
and it is the guess of my party. And we w ent to polls on that guess, and we got 
a mandate partly on this plea, that there has been a decisive, a conscious 
distortion of historical facts. 
Now, in this context, If the present Minister of Human Resource 
Development sets up a committee of eminent historians to re-examine the 
historical books, what is the grave injury that he has done to this great 
Republic? 
Sir, nobody disputes the fact that we have all to be justly proud of our 
heritage; indeed, we are But what is t he heritage that I am proud of? I am 
proud of my liberal heritage; I am proud of my secular heritage; I am proud of 
objectivity and intellectual thought; I am pr oud of a theory of history that taught 
many, many people of our generation that you cannot consciously misstate 
facts and suborn historical facts. 
Sir, this is the over-arching theme of  this debate. In this context, I ask 
myself this question, is it  not true that the highest court in this country, by two 
judges of the Apex Court, has said that it is undeniable that the institutional 
processes were suborned and that the discussions that ought to have taken 
place in the deliberative processes of NCERT and CABE, in fact, were not 
held? 
Sir, in this larger background, I ask myself these questions - 'Is the 
syllabus a syllabus which needs to be corrected? Are the History books written 
on the basis of that curriculum required to be corrected or not? And is there 
anything to suggest that this report, the re port prepared by a panel of eminent 
historians, lacks in objectivity? If the answer to all these questions is in the 
affirmative, then, we need today to endorse the decision to correct the 
distortions in History. 
Sir, in conclusion, I would only say that it was incumbent, it was 
necessary, it was politically fair and it was intellectually credible, for this 
312 

[18 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
Government to deliver on the promises it made to the people of India, in whom 
resides the ultimate sovereignty, through whom the conscience of this country speaks. 
We had made a promise to the people of India that we will, on assumption 
of power, make sure that the attempt for the colonisation of the minds of Indians will 
be resisted, and we are going to resist it, Sir, with all the force at our command, 
intellectual, physical and political. 
With these words, I thank you for giving me this opportunity. 
SHRI S. ANBALAGAN (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I rise to take 
part in the short duration discussion, and put forth my views on the change of text 
books in the school curriculum. It is my bounden duty to express my deep sense 
of gratitude to the Hon'ble Chief Minister of Tamilnadu, Dr. Puratchi Thalaivi Amma 
for sending a grass root party worker like me to this August  House. 
Sir, education is very vital for the development of a nation. Therefore, it is 
necessary to have excellent curriculum and text books. The centre should assist 
the State Governments in achieving this task. Since education is the basis for the 
future of the students, it should not be politicised. Nor should there be an attempt to 
twist history through text books. Our party is of this firm view on this. When we talk 
of curriculum and text books, we should not pick and choose a particular period for 
analysis. A lot is being said about the attempts by the centre to change history texts 
and also the curriculum too often. We fail to remember the root cause of all these 
problems. 
It all began in the year 1976. The then Congress Government shifted education 
from the state list to concurrent list. It is this concentration of power with the Union 
Government that paved the way for making arbitrary decisions. In the recent years we 
have been hearing about rewriting history. Of course, it would not be in the interest 
of the nation to distort history. AIADMK party, that I am wedded to, is of the firm 
opinion on this. But I would like to ask the Government, whether the history that has 
been taught to us is a witness to truth? With a sense of deep anguish I wish to tell the 
House that a number of great freedom fighters from Tamilnadu do not find a mention in 
our freedom history. All their names have been blacked out. The great fighter 
Veerapandia Kattampomman, the brave brothers Chinna Maruthu-Peria Maruthu, the 
Jhansi Rani of Tamilnadu Velu Naichiar, the woman   warrior   Thillaiyadi   Valliammai   
and   the   brave   patriot   Theeran

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2004] 
Chinnamali are some of the names that  are not even mentioned in Indian 
History. The Government owes a duty to tell us why they are not mentioned in 
our history. When I say this I am reminded of the great leader of the Dravidian 
movement Peraringnar Anna who, once said  on the floor of this very Hosue, 
'North Flourishes, but South perishes' I hope the 12 Ministers who are in the 
UPA Government will take steps to rectify this error. 
Sir, when we talk of education we have to refer to our education policy. 
What happened to the National educational policy announced by the Congress 
in 1986? According to that policy, by  the year 1990 all the children should 
have completed 5 years of schooling by the age of 11 and by the year 1995, 
all children were to be given free education until the age of 14 years. But all 
these promises were thrown to the winds later. 
Language is the basis for education.  But what is our policy on the 
language issue? I think even many Minist ers do not know this. This is the fact. 
The late Prime Minister Pt. Jawahar Lai Nehru gave an assurance that Hindi 
would not be imposed on the non-Hindi states. I don't think his assurance is 
being honoured. I must make one thing cl ear here. Neither we are enamoured 
of English nor are we opposed to Hindi. We only want the people to learn in 
their mother tongue in the language of the respective State. 
Sir, from the year 1986 injustice is being done to candidates seeking 
employment in Kendriya Vidhyalayas.  From drawing master to English 
teacher, the knowledge of one particular language is sought to be essential. 
Now I request that all State languages , like Tamil, Malayalm, Kannada and 
Telugu should be included in this. I say this because, I am myself a teacher 
and many teachers have discussed this with me. Sir, I wish to point out an 
aspect of various educational schemes (time bell). 
Mr. Vice Chairman, Sir, as this is my maiden speech, I request you to 
allow me a little more time. 
Sir, even the schemes are named in one particular language. The 
names of the schemes like Bhartiya Shisksha Kosh, Sarve Shiksha Abhiyan 
and so on. These names are not understood by anybody in many States. The 
Government should try to name the schemes in other languages as well. 
At this point I wish to make a reference to Tamilnadu. Tamilnadu has set 
an example in formulating education policy.   In the benign rule of Dr.

Puratchi Thalaivi Amma, Tamil Nadu Government has launched a website for 
the Education Department. And that w eb site opens with a couplet from 
Thirukural, the holybook of Tamils, a grand treatise on high morals. The 
couplet goes: 
In sandy soil when deep you delve, you reach the stream below, 
The more you learn the freer stream of wisdom flow. 
Anyone, either from Tamil Nadu or Delhi or even abroad could send 
suggestions to the Government and worthy suggestions are considered. Tamil 
Nadu is an example of how a secular and culturally compatible curriculum for 
the school could be prepared. We had so far only three aspects of study; 
prose; music and drama. But now, for the first time in India, Tamil Nadu has 
added one more aspect, that is scientific Tamil. This is being introduced from 
class I in Tamil Nadu. I think the Centre  could take steps to introduce it in 
other States as well. Environmental aw areness is also introduced to educate 
the children of our surroundings. So al so there is aids-awareness education 
that could be introduced as precautionary measure. English is also introduced 
from first standard so that students can compete in the global market. Happily, 
India is a lead player in the WTO regime. That is why China has now woken 
up to teach English to their students. China wants to develop in the area of 
software industry. Going a step ahead, Tamil Nadu has introduced bio-
chemistry, Dietetics and Nutrition, microbiology and English for 
communication in higher secondary schools. These subjects were so far the 
exclusive domain of the college curriculum. Special coaching is given to 
SC/ST students in Tamil Nadu. The SC /ST girl students are given free 
bicycles for attending school. 
From this year, free cycles are given to BC, MBC and Denotified 
community students as well.   During the last three years, 1,54,410 students 
have received the benefit at a cost of 22 crore rupees.  This year at a cost of 
Rs. 8 crore 8,50,50,000   students received the benefit. At a cost of 47 crore 
rupees, 29.600 MBC girl students received the benefit. 
Sir, I wish to make a few short points. While discussing curriculum and 
text books, parents and the public should also be involved. This will be helpful 
in formulating the curriculum. 
The Centre should consult The States while formulating the education 
policy in the future. I hope the Government will bear this in mind. I thank you, 
Sir, once again and conclude.

TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have analysed the shortcomings in the present 
meteorological forecasting system; 

RAJYA SABHA [19 August, 2004] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that a proposal has been formulated to procure some hi-tech 
world class equipment worth Rs. 500 crores to secure bettei overall meteorological 
forecasting and even for district-wise predictions; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and its present status? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND

of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Monsoon rainfall over the Indian peninsula is a result of several 
natural phenomena occurring across the globe. With the present day observational 
infrastructure and technology the world over, it is not possible to make predictions on 
spatial and temporal variations of the monsoon activity. However, on the basis of 
observations, patterns of rainfall across the country can be identified for making useful 
forecasts. The Indian Meteorological Department has been monitoring rainfall across 
the country since a long time and has already evolved models for forecasting the total 
seasonal rainfall as well as making short range forecast for meteorological sub-divisions. 
These forecasts have given important guidance to our operations, in particular, the 
agriculture operations. For improving forecasts, new models are always being 
introduced and used. 
(c) and (d) The process of upgradation of the observational systems is continuous. 
Better observations will help in improving the modeling for better forecasts. But as this 
process is evolutionary in nature, no time frame can be fixed for the same. Indian 
Meteorological Department (IMD) has come out with a proposal for investing Rs. 500 
Crores in some important areas for improving observations and the forecast system. The 
proposal is being submitted for consideration of the Government. As already stated 
complexities of weather patterns over the Indian sub continent make it extremely 
difficult to make forecasts about small geographical regions like Districts.

Statement 
(a) It is estimated that about 5000 Indians are presently in Iraq. At least 13 
Indians have lost their lives in Iraq in the last one-year. 
(b) and (c) Government have decided to provide all possible help to Indians in Iraq 
who want to return to India. In this connection, the Government have taken the* 
following concrete steps and steps:— 
(i) Government has instructed the Indian Missions in Iraq and its 
neighbouring countries to extend all possible assistance to the Indian 
nationals in Iraq who want to return to India. 
(ii) Government has requested the Governments of Jordan and Kuwait to issue 
transit visas for Indians returning to India from Iraq. 
(iii) Indian Mission in Baghdad has contacted the employers of Indians who 
wish to return to India to facilitate their travel out of Iraq and settlement of 
their dues by their employers. 
(iv) The Indian Embassy in Baghdad has sent its officials to some of the places in 
Iraq where the Indians are located to enquire their well-being and to 
provide assistance and guidance in case they have decided to leave 
Iraq. 
(d) and (e) On the night of 21stJuly, 2004, it was learnt from a news agency report 
that three Indian nationals identified as Antaryami Bains, Tilak Raj and Sukhdev Singh 
were among the seven persons taken hostage by an Iraqi group identified as 'The Holders of 
the Black Banners". The hostages included in addition three Kenyans and one Egyptian. They 
were all employed as heavy vechicle drivers by the Kuwait based company, Kuwait and Gulf 
Link Transport Co. (KGLTC). The kidnappers in a statement reported by the media 
demanded withdrawal of all citizens 
8 

[19 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
belonging to the countries of the hostages from Iraq including troops and an end 
to the activities of the transport company in Iraq. The Group threatened to 
behead a hostage every 72 hours unless these demands are met. 
Immediately after the hostage taking was reported, the Government 
initiated action forthwith to secure their release. Senior officials of the 
Ministry of External Affairs contacted Indian Missions in Baghdad and 
Kuwait to explore all possiblities to ensure safety of the hostages and their 
early release. Minister of State (MoS) for External Affairs, Shri E. Ahammed 
spoke to the Charged Affaires in Embassy of India, Baghdad and the Indian 
Ambassador in Kuwait. A Crisis Management Group was constituted under the 
Chairmanship of Shri Ahammed and a Control Room was made operative in 
Ministry of External Affairs. Minister of External Affairs, Shri K. Natwar 
Singh issued an appeal to the kidnappers through the Arab TV Network for 
release of the hostages who are innocent civilians and not combatants. The 
Government also contacted the Governments of Egypt and Kenya whose 
nationals are among the hostages for inputs to work for the release of the 
hostages. Our Mission in Kuwait has been in touch with the transport company 
KGL from the very beginning of the abduction and received and assured the 
company that it will take all possible steps to secure release and safe return of 
the kidnapped drivers. 
The situation is constantly being monitored by the Crisis Management 
Group which meets several times a day to review strategies to secure safe and 
early release of hostages. Shri E. Ah ammed, MOS has issued two appeals to 
the kidnappers through Arabic TV network highlighting historical relations 
between India and Iraq and India's well-known and principled position and 
concern for the welfare and well being of Iraqi people and their country and 
requesting for immediate release of the hostages. He also made an appeal to the 
captors in Arabic language for release of the hostages on humanitarian grounds. 
Religious leaders in Iraq and other Gulf countries were contacted to intercede 
for the release of the hostages. Ambassador of India in Muscat, Shri Talmiz 
Ahmad alongwith an Arabic interpreter has been deputed to Iraq to monitor and 
report on the development and to assist in the work of the Indian mission for 
early and safe release of the hostages. Cabinet Secretary chaired several 
meetings to review the situation and the ongoing efforts to secure the release of 
the hostages. Prime Minister held a meeting to

followed the development closely and gave directions whenever necessary.

Statement 
Private Investment in Nuclear Energy Sector 
(a) and (b) The Atomic Energy Act 1962, as amended in 1987, allows setting 
up of Nuclear Power Plants only by Government or Government companies in 
which not less than 51% equity is held by the Central Government. At 
present the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL) and Bharatiya 
Nabhakiya Vidyut Nigam (BHAVINI) are the two Public Sector Companies in 
the field of Nuclear Power. Both these companies are owned 100% by 
Government of India.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI SURESH PACHOURI): (a) 
Computer Science and Engineering is not included as an independent subject in 
the Combined Engineering Services Examination and the Civil Services 
Examination. 
(b) Article 320 of the Constitution of India states that it shall be the 
duty of the Union Public Service Commission, to conduct examinations 
for appointment to the services of the Union. The recruitment procedure 
for Combined Engineering Services Examination and the Civil Services 
Examination, conducted by the Union Public Service Commission is as 
below. 
(i) Combined Engineering Services Examination:— 
The Combined Engineering Services Examination is conducted in two 
stages, the written examination followe d by Personality Test, a candidate is 
required to select one of four specified Engineering disciplines. The written 
Examination comprises two sections-Section I consisting only of objective type 
of questions and Section II of conventional papers. Both sections cover the entire 
syllabus of the relevant engineering discipline viz. Civil Engineering, 
Mechanical Engineering, Electrical & Electronic and Telecommunications 
Engineering. 
(ii) Civil Services Examination:— 
The Civil Services Examination co mprises three stages, namely the 
Preliminary Examination, the Main Examination and the Interview for 
Personality test. A candidates has to opt for two optional subjects among a list of 
51 optional subject, including 26 languages. The list also offers Civil 
Engineering, Electrical Engineering and Mechanical Engineering as optional 
Subjects. Computer Science is, however, not included in the list of optional 
subjects.

TECHNOLOGY (SHRI DAYANIDHI MARAN): (a) The

cellular operators including BSNL & MTNL to fix tariffs. Thus, the operators are

usage pattern. There are a large number of tariff plans offered by MTNL, BSNL

charge of Rs. 1.90 to 3.90 per minute depending upon distance & type of 
terminating network with 60 seconds pul se and national SMS charge of Rs. 
1.50 per message. The private operator has a plan of

FDI in mining sector 
1628. SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Government have approved about Rs. 
4,000 crores of foreign direct investment in mining sector; 
57 

RAJYA SABHA [19 August, 2004] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the country had been deficient in high value minerals 
because of low investment and lack of  advanced technology required for 
detailed exploration; 
(d) whether Government are considering to provide incentives to boost 
private investment and to make industry more productive and competitive; 
and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL AND 
MINES (DR. DASARI NARAYAN RAO): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB), in consultation with 
the Department of Mines, has so far approved 73 proposals of Foreign Direct 
Investment (FDI) in the mining sector. The likely investment in these cases 
will be about Rs.4,044 crores. The approval granted by FIPB is only for foreign 
equity participation in a company incorporated in India. After obtaining FIPB 
approval these companies are required to apply to the concerned State 
Governments, which are the owners of minerals in their respective territorial 
jurisdictions for mineral concessions. 
(c) Yes, Sir. The geological setting and metallogenitic history of India is 
similar to mineral rich Australia, South Africa and Antarctica. However, due to 
low investment and lack of advanced state-of-the-art technology for detailed 
exploration, deep-seated high value minerals like gold, diamond, base metals, 
etc. have not yet been fully discovered. 
(d) and (e) The Government already offers a wide range of incentives to 
investors in India, engaged in mining activities. The entire non-atomic and non-
fuel mining sector is now open for private investment including Foreign Direct 
Investment (FDI). A hundred per cent FDI is permitted for mineral exploration 
through the automatic route except diamonds and precious stones where 
100% is permitted through Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB). The 
other incentives inter alia include (a) availability of tax holiday; (b) 
depreciation allowances on mining and quarrying equipments, environment 
protection equipment, pollution control equipment, energy saving equipment, 
etc.; (c) deduction in respect of export turnover; and (d) limited deduction of 
expenditure on prospecting, extraction and production of minerals from the 
total income.

Circulation of counterfeit postal stamps etc. 
1641. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of COMMUNI 
CATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
71 

RAJYA SABHA [19 August, 2004] 
(a) the details of the instances of detection of circulation of counterfeit postal stamps 
and circulation/encashments of fake Postal Orders, National Saving Certificates, 
Kisan Vikas Patras and other small saving instruments dealt with by the Post Offices in 
the country, till date; and 
(b) the steps taken, if any, for precaution, prevention and detection of circulation 
of counterfeit postal stamps and other valued postal instruments, besides these small 
saving certificates? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. 
SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) Some cases of circulation of counterfeit postal ,stamps in 
various parts of the country have come to the notice of the Department since 1999. Till 
date counterfeit stamps valued at more than Rs. 6,00,00,000/- (Rupees six crores only) 
have been detected/seized. Reported instances of fake stamps are given in the enclosed 
Statement (See below) 
No case of fake Postal Orders, National Saving Certificates, Kisan Vikas Patras 
and other small Savings instruments has come to notice. 
(b) The following precautions/preventive steps have been taken by the 
Department:— 
(i) Instructions have been issued to all the Heads of Postal Circles for 
conducting surpise checks/visits for checking the stamps Vendors/Post 
Office Treasuries, Circle Stamps Depots (CSDs). 
(ii) Instructions to Heads of Circles for activating Circle/Regional Checking 
Squads and checking of Licensed Stamps Vendors/ Licensed Postal 
Agents/Panchayat Sanchar Sewa Kendras have been issued. 
(iii) Staff have been made aware of the features of genuine stamps like 
quality of paper and colour of print, perforation, watermark and quality 
and colour of gumming so that they can identify and detect fake stamps 
from the genuine ones. 
(iv) Heads of Circles have been instructed to give publicity requesting the 
public to purchase stamps only from Post Offices or authorized agents 
and not from any other source. 
72 

[19 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(v) Field units have been instructed to book the articles through Multi 
Purpose Counter Machines (MPCMs ), wherever such machines 
are available, in order to reduce the need to use stamps. 
(vi) Use of franking machines by institutional customers is being 
encouraged. 
(vii) Since February, 2004, technical data of commemorative stamps is 
also not published.

NORMS FOR OPENING POST OFFICES:                                                   
1. Norms for opening Extra Departmental Branch Post Offices:                                     
1.1 Population:

villages.

1.2 Distance: 
(a) In Normal Areas: 
The minimum distance from the near est existing post office will be 3 
Kms. 
(b) In Hilly, Tribal Desert and Inaccessible Areas: 
The distance limit will be the same as above except that in Hilly Areas, 
the minimum distance limit can be relaxed by the Directorate in cases where 
such relaxation is warranted by special circumstances which should be clearly 
explained while submitted a proposal. 
1.3 Anticipated Income: 
(a) In Normal Areas: 
The minimum anticipated revenue will be 33V3% of the cost. 
(b) In Hilly, Tribal, Desert and Inaccessible Areas: 
The minimum anticipated income will be 15% of the cost. 2. Criteria for 
upgrading/opening Departmental Sub Post Offices: 
(c) In Rural Areas: 
The minimum work load of the Ex tra Departmental Branch Post 
Office, proposed to be upgraded, should be five hours per day. 
The permissible limit of annual loss is Rs. 2400/- in Normal Rural 
Areas and Rs. 4800/- in Tribal and Hilly areas. 
(d) In Urban Areas: 
In Urban areas, the post office should initially be self-supporting, and, at 
the time of the first annual review, it should show a 5% profit to be eligible for 
further retention. 
The minimum distance between two post offices should be 1.5 Kms. in 
cities with a population of 20 lakhs and above, and 2 Kms. in other Urban 
Areas. No two delivery offices, however, should be closer than 5 Kms. for 
each other. 
Heads of Circles have powers to relax the distance condition in 10% of 
the cases. 
A Delivery Post Office in Urban Area should have a minimum of 7 
Postmen's beats.

Steps taken by the Government to promote the Hardware Sector 
1. Peak rate of customs duty continues to be 20%. Customs duty on project

@10%. Customs duty on Computers and Peripherals is @10%. All 
storage devices, integrated circuits, microprocessors, data display tubes 
and deflection components of colour monitors continue at 0%. Customs duty 
on Information Technology Agreement (ITA-1) bound items is as per 
commitments. Customs duty on parts of computers and SMPS has been fully 
exempted. Customs Duty on specified raw materials/inputs used for 
manufacture of electronic components or optical fibres/cables is @ 0%. 
Customs duty on specified capital goods used for manufacture of electronic 
goods is @ 0%. Specified infrastructure equipment for basic/ 
cellular/internet, V-SAT, radio paging and public mobile radio trunked 
services and parts of such equipment exempted from basic customs duty. 
Customs duty exemption to mobile switching centres presently 
available to cellular mobile telephone service providers has been 
extended to imports by universal access service providers. Customs duty 
on cell phones continues at 5%. Laptops brought as part of baggage are 
exempted from customs duty. 
2. Export Promotion Capital Goods Scheme (EPCG) allows capital goods 
on payment of 5% customs duty. The Export Obligation under the scheme 
is linked to the duty saved and is 8 times the duty saved on capital goods

Prediction of monsoon and drought situation 
1771. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Meteorological Department is not well-
equipped to predict the arrival of Monsoon or the drought situation; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to improve the Meteorological 
Department? 
THE MiNISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) No, Sir. IMD is fairly 
equipped to predict the arrival of mons oon and also the quantum of rainfall 
expected during the season as a whole which include the probability of drought 
also. However, the intra-seasonal variability, both in space and time, is not 
well understood due to lack of high resolution numerical models, especially 
tuned to tropical weather condition and matching high resolution weather data. 
(c) A comprehensive review of the infrastructure required for achieving 
high resolution weather forecast both, in time and space, was carried out. A 
proposal to upgrade technology for effecting improvement in observing, 
forecasting, product generation and dissemination system is being submitted for 
consideration by the Government. 
Failure of Meteorological Department in prediction 
1772. SHRI DATTA MEGHE: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Meteorological Department has badly failed 
in forecasting weather and its estimates have always been proving wrong; 
184 

[19 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor, 
(c) whether any measures have been ta ken to ensure correct forecasts 
by the Meteorological Department; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) No, Sir. IMD has been 
using 16-parameter Power Regression Model for issuing Long Range 
Forecast of total quantum of rainfall likely during the season as a whole since 
1988. Its performance was seen to be satisfactory and was appreciated until 
2002 when the model could not capture the large deficiency of rainfall. 
(b) Monsoon is a complex phenomenon involving land, ocean and 
atmosphere. It originates as a result of  series of energy exchanges occurring 
in the earth atmosphere system. Though  attempts have been made over the 
year to unravel the mysteries of development and strengthening of monsoon, 
the complex interactions leading to energy exchange are not well understood. 
There is no technology anywhere in the world to give exact forecast of 
monsoon like systems. 
(c) and (d) Attempts were made to refine and introduce a number of 
new models before commencement of 2003 monsoon. These models gave 
fairly accurate forecasts for the seas on and also for the month of July 2003. 
However, based on the same models, the forecasts for rainfall in July 2004 has 
not Materialized as the realised rainfall was 81% compared to 98+9% 
forecasted rainfall. Seasonal rainfall forecast is 100+4%. The performance for 
the season will be assessed after the season is over. IMD in collaboration with 
Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore has implemented a Numerical Weather 
Prediction (NWP) system for the seasonal prediction of monsoon rainfall. 
Currently the NWP system is in the experimental mode and some 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [19 August, 2004] 
more research work is necessary before it is made operational. In the meantime, IMD 
is working sincerely for the further improvement of the statistical models.

RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2004] 
Statement 
(a) to (f) There was a break in the progress and intensity of the South-
West Monsoon over many parts of the country during July this year. While 
there was a revival in Andhra Pradesh around the middle of that month, many 
States, particularly, Maharashtra, Gu jarat, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan 
remained in serious deficits till 28th July when the cumulative deficit for the 
country as a whole was —15%. After that date there has been a general 
revival, and the country-wide deficit has come down to -10% on 4th August 
and to — 7% on 11th August. Considerable improvement has occurred in 
some of the above areas. This revival has caused an upsurge in sowing and a 
general improvement of agricultural prospects. As kharif sowing is still in 
progress it will be premature at this state to estimate reduction in kharif 
production. 
Central Government is in touch with the States. The situation is being 
closely and constantly monitored. To enable States to have ready availability of 
funds to deal with any eventuality at the earliest, Rs. 498.77 crores have been 
sanctioned (including Rs. 25.84 crores recommended for Jharkhand) in advance 
from the Calamity Relief Fund (CRF) of States with major rainfall deficits in July. 
Based on preliminary reports from these States, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh 
have been allocated 1 lakh and 0.50 lakh MTs of foodgrains respectively to 
initiate relief employment. Railways are transporting water, free of cost, to 
the affected towns in Rajasthan.

Special arrangement for SC Community under National Health 
Policy 
†*365. SHRI NARAYAN SINGH KESRI: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELAFRE be pleased to state 
(a) whether any special arrangement has been made for rural scheduled 
caste community under National Health Policy; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, whether Government would consider for special arrangement 
for crores of the scheduled caste population in rural areas of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The National Health Policy-2002 gives overriding 
importance to ensuring a more equitable access to health services across the social 
expanse of the country. In order to meet the objective of reducing such inequities 
and imbalances between economic classes and allow the disadvantaged 
section of society a fairer access to pub lic health services, the Policy envisages 
to increase the sectoral outlay in the primary health sector. Further, the Policy 
also emphasises that the state Government will need to design separate 
schemes, wherever required, tailor-m ade to the health  needs of socio-
economically under-served sections of population under the overall umbrella 
of macro-policy prescriptions contained in the National Health Policy, 2002. 
(c) Health is a state subject and State Governments are primarily 
responsible for provision of health care for the citizenry at large including the 
rural scheduled caste population.Government of India is, however, 
implementing the National Health Programmes for control of major 
communicable and non-communicable dis eases like Malaria, TB, Leprosy, 
AIDS, Blindness, Cancer and Mental Health which covers the entire country, 
including the scheduled caste population, both in urban and rural areas. Also, the 
Government proposes to redesign the Universal Health Insurance Scheme 
exclusively for Below Poverty Line (BPL) families and also enhance the 
premium subsidy. The restructured scheme shall largely benefit the scheduled 
caste families as majority of them would be covered under the BPL category.

Under the provision of Drugs and Cosmetics Act,. 1940, and rules

company/manufacturing companies in the small, medium or large sectors. 
Information pertaining to details of the licensed companies which have no 
manufacturing base in the country and get their products manufactured on loan

†*363. SHRI PYARELAL KHANDEL WAL: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government's health service, continuing 
under the National Health Policy, has failed to achieve its goals; 
(b) if so, the reaction of Government in this regard; and 
(c) if not, the number of health centres opened so far across the country 
under the National Health Policy and their present status. 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) and (b) Public Health initiatives over the years 
have contributed significantly to the progressive improvement of various health 
indicators. These include demographic changes reflected by increased life 
expectancy, reduction in crude birth and death rates and infant mortality rates; 
epidemiological shifts in terms of eradication of small pox and guinea worm, 
containment of number of cases of communicable diseases like malaria and 
leprosy; growth in infrastructure in terms of increase in number of Sub-Centres 
(SCs)/Primary Health Centres (PHCs) /Community Health Centres (CHCs), 
dispensaries, hospitals and beds as also medical personnel including doctors 
and nurses. These improvements show that  the health servi ces created in the 
country have not failed to achieve their goals. 
This various time-bound goals set in the National Health Policy— 2002 
are annexed as Statement (See below). Out of the various goals specified, four 
of them relate to the year 2005. These include eradication 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2004] 
of polio and yaws, elimination of leprosy, establishing an integrated system of 
surveillance, national health accounts and health statistics and increase state sector 
health spending from 5.5% to 7% of the budget. Polio and yaws are on the 
verge of being eradicated and leprosy has reached near elimination level with 17 
States already having achieved it and 7 States close to achieving the same. An 
integrated disease surveillance programme has been launched to cover the 
entire country in a phased manner. A system of national health accounts is in the 
progress of being established. The goal regarding increasing the State sector 
health spending was discussed in the last conference of Central Council of Health 
& Family Welfare held in August, 2003 and States were accordingly 
requested to take apporpriate action on this. 
(c) A three-tier Primary Health Care system consisting of SCs, PHCs 
and CHCs has been established in the countrty, 1,37,311 SCs, 22,926 PHCs 
and 3,106 CHCs are currently functioning in the country. An additional 8,669 
new SCs are in the process of being opened during the Tenth Plan based on the 
norms as per the census data of 1991 taking the total number of SCs to 
1,45,980 by 2006-07. The status of health centres varies across States with 
regard to availability of medical and paramedical manpower, medicines and 
consumables and building housing such centres. Presently, there is a shortage of 
around 16%, 19% and 54%, in number of SCs, PHCs and CHCs respectively 
vis-a-vis the population norms of 2001 Census across the country. There is 
also a shortage of around 15% of Auxiliary Nurse Mid-wives in SCs and PHCs 
and 49% in Health Worker (Male) at the Sub-Centre level; the shortage in 
doctors at the PHC level is around 8% wh ere as that of specialists at the CHC 
level is 61%.

*372. SHRI K. CHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether according to World Health  Organisation the country with 
highest number of maternal deaths is India; 
(b) whether any policy has been formulated/targeted for safe

34 

[20 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) the details of maternal deaths for the last three years, State-wise, 
year-wise; and 
(e) the number of Primary Health Centres in rural and Urban areas which 
are equipped to deal with emergencies in cases of child birth State-wise, as on 
today? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (e) According to the estimates of Maternal 
mortality published by WHO in their publication, "Maternal Mortality-2000" 
it has been estimated that 529,000 women die every year globally as a result of 
complications arising from pregnancy and childbirth. According to the same 
report, 136,000 of these are estimated to be in India. However, based on the 
maternal mortality ratios of countries, published in the same report, 42 
countries have maternal mortality ratio higher than that of India. 
Maternal health care is an integr al part of the Family Welfare 
Programme. Certain vertical interventions like the National Nuritional 
Anaemia Control Programme and Tetanus Immunization Programme for 
pregnant mothers have been going on under the Family Welfare Programme 
since 1977-78. In 1992, the nationwide Child Survival and Safe Motherhood 
(CSSM) (1992—97) was launched with World Bank support, for integrating 
various vertical interventions in the area of Maternal and Child Health. 
The ongoing Reproductive and Child Health Programme is being 
implemented in all States/Union Territori es since 1997 and aims at bringing 
down the maternal mortality and morbidity. Under this programme, various 
interventions focused on reducing maternal deaths are being implemented. 
These are essential obstetric care; Emergency Obsetric Care; provision for 
referral transport for pregnant women with complication of pregnancy through 
panchayats; provision of drugs and equipment at first referral units; provision 
of contractual staff like Additional Hea lth Workers, Staff Nurses, Laboratory 
Technicians and hiring of Anesthetists from private sector for provision of 
emergency obstetric care. Funds are also being provided for schemes like 24 
hours delivery services at selected primary health centres and community 
health centres; training of dais in all districts of EAG States and selected 
districts in other States where safe delivery rate is less then 
35 

RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2004] 
30 per cent. Funds are also provided for organizing Reproductive and Child 
Health camps in remote and underutilised Primary Health Centres in all 
districts of EAG States. 
Under the existing National Maternity Benefit Scheme, pregnant 
women belonging to Below Poverty Line (BPL) families are being assisted for

Public spending on health in India 
*373.   SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: 
SHRI DATTA MEGHE: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether according to data available in Human Development Report, 
2004 India ranks 171 out of 175 countries in terms of public spending on 
health; 
(b) if so, whether public spending on health in India is a mere 0.9 per 
cent of GDP; 
(c) whether according to the Planning Commission's latest review, there 
is just one doctor for 1008 people and one bed for 1223 of the population; 
(d) if so, whether there is shortage of more than 42,000 doctors in 
Government run hospitals; and 
(e) the steps Government propose to take to meet the shortage and also 
improve health spending in India? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (e) Although no ranking of countries is given 
for public spending on health in the Human Development Report 2004, based on 
data given in the Report, it is seen that India ranks 171 out of 175 countries in 
terms of public spending on health. According to this Report, the total health 
expenditure as a % of GDP in India is 5.1 % of which 0.9% of GDP is the share 
of public health expenditure in the year 2001. 
Planning Commission has only done an internal review of the health sector 
based on data/information supplied by the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare. As per the statistics worked out by the Medical Council of India, the 
availability of allopathic doctors is at present in the ratio 1:1800. If the 
practitioners of Indian System of Medicine and Homoeopathy are also taken into 
account, the ratio of availability of doctors to the population improves to 1:800. 
Similarly, the population bed ratio (allopathic beds) is 1:1503 i.e. one bed for 
1503 persons as on 1.1.2002. This improves to 1:1124 if all types of beds are 
considered. 
41 

RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2004] 
The Central Government hospitals are manned by doctors from Central 
Health Services (CHS) cadre, which has about 850 vacant posts against a 
sanctioned strength of about 4700 doctors. In so far as hospitals run by the State 
Governments are concerned, norms regarding requirement of doctors have 
been prescribed for Primary Health Centres (PHCs) and Community Health 
Centres (CHCs). As per information available up to March, 2002, there is a 
shortage of 1779 doctors at PHCs vis-a-vis the norms in 8 States across the 
country. However, at the CHC level, shortage of about 7500 specialists have 
been reported by all the State Governments vis-a-vis the norms. In addition, 
there are hospitals at the sub-district/district and the State level. The filling up 
of posts of doctors in such hospitals falls under the purview of State 
Governments and no norms have been prescribed for them by the Centre. 
The Central Government has adopted the policy of downsizing its staff 
strength. Department of Health has taken up the matter for seeking exemption of 
technical/scientific posts of the health sector (which includes all CHS posts) from 
the purview of instructions of Department of Personnel and Training under this 
policy. Assistance is provided to the States for engaging private anaesthetists 
and doctors trained in Medical Termination of Pregnancy techniques on 
contractual basis, to take care of emergency obstetric care and alleviate the 
shortage of trained manpower at the CHC level. Government is making all out 
efforts to increase expenditure on health subejct to sectoral priorities and 
overall budetary resources. External assistance from bilateral and multilateral 
agencies is also mobilised to augment the resources for the health sector. The 
National Common Minimum Programme envisages increasing public 
spending on health to at least 2-3% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) over 
the next 5 years. The National Health Policy-2002 also envisages inceasing 
public health investment to 2% of GDP by 2010. To achieve this, the Health 
Policy stipulates increasing the expenditure on health by state Governments to 
7% of their budget by 2005 and to 8% of their budget by 2010. The Policy 
further envisages to raise the Central Government's contribution to States 
from 15% to 25% by 2010.

*377. SHRI MAM. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) to what extent the National Surveillance Programme of 
Communicable Diseases has been effective not only in controlling and 
preventing communicable diseases but also in helping to forecast the 
outbreak of epidemics; 
(b) the details with reference to some specific instances, State-wise; 
(c) whether the World Bank has extended its support to this 
programme in terms of financial aid and technical and professional expertise; 
and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (d) Na tional Surveillance Programme for 
Communicable Diseases (NSPCD) was launched as a Central Sector Health 
Programme during the year 1997-98 and is operational in 101 districts of all 
States and Union Territories. 
During this period, as part of the programme strategy, multidi-
sciplinary teams called Rapid Response Teams (RRTs) were constituted both at 
the State level and in all the programme districts. The RRTs have trained 
medical & paramedical workers at the di strict and sub-district levels in 
disease surveillance. Existing laboratories  have also been strengthened in all 
the 101 programme districts and in 21 States at the State level. These 
laboratories perform routine laboratory surveillance as well as support 
outbreak investigations, wherever possible. 
The RRTs under NSPCD, apart from performing the routine 
surveillance for communicable diseases, have identified outbreaks early and 
managed them on their own and at the same time prevented and helped reduce 
the mortality and morbidity, thus striving to make the districts and the States self-
reliant in the process. They have also supported investigations of larger 
outbreaks both at the State and national level and even in non-NSPCD districts. 
Currently there are 118 State RRT members and 251 district RRT members 
trained under the programme. During

established under NSPCD, details of which are annexed as Statement (See 
below). These included large outbreaks of Leptospirosis and Dengue in Kerala 
and Viral Encephalitis in Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh. 
Laboratory support was provided by the NSPCD laboratories in more than 
50% of these outbreaks. 
An Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) is proposed to be 
implemented in the country in a phased manner. The World Bank will provide a 
soft credit of US $ 68 million during 2004—2009 for various activities under 
IDSP. Main components of the project are:— 
(a) To establish an integrated and decentraliszed State-based system for 
surveillance for communicable and non-communicable diseases for 
improving the efficiency of existing surveillance activities; 
(b) Strengthening of public health laboratories for diagnosis of various 
diseases and epidemic investigations; 
(c) Establishment of information technology network for timely data 
transmission and analysis; 
(d) Training of personnel in disease surveillance; and 
(e) Undertaking surveys to assess risk factors for non-communicable 
diseases.

*379. SHRI UDAY PRATAP SINGH: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the anti-diabetic drug "Phenformin" was banned in the 
United States in 1971; 
(b) whether this drug is continued to be manufactured and sold in India; 
and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the names of the companies 
manufacturing this product in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) the drug 'Phenformin' was withdrawn in 
USA in 1971 because of reported occurrence of lactic acidosis in some 
patients with the use of the drug. The matter was also examined in consultation 
with Experts in India during early eighties. It was opined by the Experts that 
lactic acidosis reported in the West is not common in Indian Population and the 
drug was effective as an oral antidiabetic drug. Therefore, the drug was not 
withdrawn or banned in the country. However, the issue concerning 
continued use of Phenformin has been re viewed in light of fact that new and 
better oral anti-diabetic drugs are now available. The matter was then re-
examined by the Drug Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) in its 52nd meeting 
which was held on 10th April, 2003 and after detailed deliberation, DTAB 
recommended withdrawal of Phenformin.

Special package to agriculture sector 
1790. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOO T: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have decided to give a special 
package to agriculture sector in order to boost agricultural production in the 
country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the target expected to be achieved in respect of agriculture produce 
during the current financial year; and 
(d) the contingency plan thought of in the event of shortfall in 
production? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) In order to increase the agriculture 
production in the country, the Tenth Five Year Plan as well as Annual Plans 
are formulated by the Department which contains a number of programmes & 
interventions, the major schemes are indicated below:— 
— Macro Management of Agriculture consisting of 27 schemes for 
production of cereals and coarse cereals, sugarcane, jute, watershed 
development, horticulture and cooperation. 
— On Farm Water Management for increasing Crop Production in 
eastern India. 
—  Technology Mission on Cotton. 
— Technology Mission on Coconut. 
— Technology Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture in 
North Eastern States Including Sikkim, Jammu & Kashmir, 
Himachal Pradesh & Uttaranchal. 
— Integrated Scheme of Oilseeds, Pulses, Oil Palm & Maize 
(ISOPOM). 
Under Risk Management, a number of schemes like National 
Agriculture Insurance Scheme, Farm Income Insurance Scheme, Minimum 
Support Price, Market Intervention Scheme as a safety nets 
67 

RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2004] 
for the farmers are being implemente d. More recently, Government has 
announced a number of initiatives to enhance credit availability to the farm 
sector. 
In the field of marketing & storage and to address the problems of post 
harvest management, Government is implementing schemes for Construction 
of Cold Storages, Rural Godowns and Development of Market Infrastructure, 
Grading and Standardization. 
To promote agricultural extension, department is implementing the 
schemes of Kisan Call Centre, Mass Media Support to Agriculture Extension, 
establishment of Agri-Clinics and Agri- Business by Agriculture Graduates. 
Annual Plans formulated by the department are comprehensive and cover 
all aspects of the agriculture production. In the current Annual Plan 2004-05, and 
outlay of Rs. 265.00 crores has been provided. 
(c) and (d) Agriculture production is highly dependent on weather 
conditions. There are two main cropping seasons viz. Kharif and Rabi. 
Different crops are grown in these seasons. Therefore, it is too early to assess 
the achievement of crop production during the current financial year and the 
shortfall in production. However, the Government maintains a buffer stock of 
food grains in order to meet the shortfall in the production.

Clean coal technology based fertilizer plants 
1812. SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHER JEE: Will the Minister of 
CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a number of power and fertilizer plants in other countries are 
running on clean coal technology/coal gassification process; 
(b) whether eight such plants are under implementation in China alone; 
(c) whether Government are considering implementation of such project 
in the country, 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; 
85 

RAJYA SABHA  . [20 August, 2004] 
(e) whether possibilities of revival of coal based fertilizer plants or 
retrofitting Naphtha based fertilizer plan ts with coal gassification process is 
being looked into; and 
(f) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) and (b) A number of coal based fertilizer plants are 
operating in other countries and there are four coal based ammonia plants with 
capacities above 1000 tonnes per day under implementation in China. A few 
power plants based on integrated Coal  Gasification Combined Cycle (IGCC) 
technology are also in operation in other countries. The coal gasification 
technology is in the demonstration stage in these countries and is yet to prove as 
a commercially viable option for power generation. There is no specific 
information on the number of power plants under implementation in China 
using this technology. The coal gasification technology is yet to be 
demonstrated for the high ash Indian coals. 
(c) to (f) The Government has not so far received any proposal for setting 
up fertilizer plants based on synthesis gas from coal gassification in the country. 
In the event of synthesis gas from coal gasification being available in adequate 
quantities at economical rates for fertilizer production, the techno-economic 
feasibility of setting up new plants or revival/retrofitting of existing coal and 
naphtha based plants based on this as feedstock would have to be established in 
the light of the fact that indigenous coal has high ash content and its 
beneficiation/washing to bring down ash condent may involve high operational 
costs. In the power sector, pilot coal gasification projects have been established 
at Indian Institute of Chemical Technology and Bharat Heavy Electrical Ltd. 
(BHEL), both at Hyderabad. BHEL has set up 6.2 MW IGCC pilot plant at 
Tiruchi to demonstrate the technology. Efforts are on to set up an IGCC project 
to demonstrate the technology using high ash Indian coal. In this regard an inter 
Ministerial Steering Group under the Chairmanship of Secretary (Power) has 
been constituted for monitoring the implementation of 100 MW IGCC 
demonstration project. This project is proposed to be put up as a joint venfure 
between BHEL and NTPC. Auraiya Gas Power Station of NTPC has been 
selected for setting up this demonstration project.

considered reasonable without detailed i nvestigation. Each and every case is

1837. SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIK AR: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware th at more than 100 million metric 
tonnes of fly ash from thermal power plants and 10 million tonnes of 
blast furnace slag from steel plan ts constitute a major environmental 
hazard; 
(b) if so, to what extent the cement industry is utilising these 
hazardous wastes to curtail use of conventional limest one and gypsum; 
and 
(c) the measures being taken to attain optimum utilisation of fly ash 
and furnace slag? 
113 

RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2004] 
. THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Both the fly ash 
and blast furnace slag generated by Thermal Power Plants and Steel Plants respectively 
constitute an environmental concern and problem. About 12 million tonnes of fly ash and 
5 million tonnes of blast furnace slag are being used by the cement industry. 
(c) Government of India has issued a Notification in September, 1999 which 
inter alia stipulates the use of fly ash by building and road construction agencies. The 
Notification envisages utilising the entire fly ash generated by the Thermal Power Plants 
in 9/15 years. A number of Thermal Power Plants have established facilities for collection 
of storage of dry fly ash wherever required. The Bureau of Indian Standards has revised 
its specification for use of fly ash in cement from 25% to 35%. Bureau of Indian 
Standards has also published standards for use of Portland blast furnace slag cement 
which permits use of granulated slag from steel plant up to 75% in the cement 
manufacture. The Indian Road Congress has published the standards for use of fly ash 
in the road construction. A number of State Governments have included fly ash bricks/ 
products/pozzolona cement in their specifications, schedules and tender documents. Fly 
ash utilisation programme of Department of Science and Technology also facilitates 
demonstration projects on manufacture of fly ash bricks and back filling of underground 
coal mines with fly ash. Building Material Technology Promotion Council of Ministry of 
Urban Development conducts awareness programme on use of fly ash bricks/products 
in building construction. Central Government is continuously monitoring the utilisation of 
fly ash and has asked the steel industry to study the back filling of mines with blast 
furnace slag. The State Governments have also constituted monitoring committee to 
monitor the use of fly ash by different sectors.

Decline in the child sex ratio is a concern for all. The United Nations

Observation of C&AG on HIV infected patients 
1856. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed a recent observation of the 
Comptroller and Auditor General of India highlighting inter alia that a large 
number of HIV infected patients are not being revealed the actual status of 
their disease which could lead to such persons unknowingly spreading the 
disease among the un-infected persons and the NACO has failed to discharge 
its due obligations in this regard; and 
(b) if so, the details of steps being taken for proper implmentation of the 
HIV/AIDS control programme for timely prevention and treatment of the 
disease? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) 
HIV testing is being done at voluntary counselling and testing centers and for 
Prevention of Parent to Child Transmission located at antenatal clinics 
established in identified hospitals. Testing is done on voluntary basis after pre 
test counselling and consent of the person is taken before testing. The person 
is called in between 1 to 7 days period to collect the report which is given 
after post test counselling for both HIV positive and HIV negative persons. If 
the HIV positive person do not come to collect the report, the report is not 
sent to the patient as the test is done at the district hospital and medical 
colleges. Moreover, confidentiality of the test result has to be maintained. 
Some hospital counsellor do write to the positive person to report to the 
hospital without revealing the report in the letter. For research purposes 
including surveillance, the testing is being done on unlinked and anonymous 
basis in order to minimise participation and selection bias in sampling. 
Detailed guidelines on Voluntary Counseling and Testing and National Blood 
Policy have been formulated and distributed for implementation under the 
programme.

centers and community health centers, training of dais in all districts of EAG States and 
selected districts in other States where safe delivery rate is less than 30 per cent. Funds are 
also provided for organizing Reproductive and Child Health camps in remote and 
underutilized Primary Health Centers in all districts of EAG States.

assistance to States/UTs for extending financial assistance at the rate of Rs. 500/- per

1876.    SHRI ABANI ROY: 
                            SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA:

(a) the total number of samples of drugs that have been lifted by drug 
inspectors during the last three years all over the country, year-wise; 
160 

[20 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) the details of percentage of samples declared spurious and the names 
of persons/Licensed companies manufacturing these drugs; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to stop the negative publicity of 
spurious drugs? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) As 
per feed back available from Drugs Control Administrations of States UTs, 
38834, 36314 & 40862 drug samples were tested during 2001-02, 2002-03 and 
2003-04, out of which 96,125 and 118 samples respectively were found spurious 
which is 0.25, 0.34 and 0.29 percent of the total samples tested. 
Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and rules thereunder, the 
responsibility for regulating manufacture and sale of drugs including taking 
administrative and legal action against the manufacturers tests with the State 
Governments. Based on the gravity of the offences detected, necessary punitive 
action under the said Act and rules is taken against the manufacturers for such 
categories of drugs by the concerned Drugs Controllers. In view of this, specific 
details of the spurious drugs detected etc. together with their identified 
manufacturers are not maintained centrally. 
(c) In view of the media reports quoting varying figures about the extent 
of circulation of spurious drugs in the country, the Government took a serious 
note of such reports and constituted an expert committee under the 
chairmanship of Dr. R.A. Mashelkar in January, 2003 to undertake a 
comprehensive examination of drug regulatory issues including spurious drugs 
in the country. Based on the recommendations of Dr. R.A. Mashelkar 
Committee, a legislation to amend the penal provisions of Drugs and 
Cosmetics Act, 1940 and to provide for stricter penalties to the offenders 
including a maximum penalty of capital punishment was introduced in the 
Parliament in December, 2003. The said legislation lapsed with the dissolution 
of the Parliament. The steps to introduce the said legislation again have been 
initiated. The salient amendments proposed under the Bill are given below— 
(1) Enhancement punishments relating to spurious or adulterated drugs 
leading to death or grievous hurt within the meaning of Section 320 IPC upto 
punishment of death or imprisonment for a term which 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2004] 
shall not be less than 10 years but which may extend to imprisonment for life and 
shall also be liable to fine or one lakh rupees or upto 3 times the value of the 
goods seized, whichever is higher. 
(2) Penalties for subsequent offences to be enhanced upto 10 years and with 
fine which shall not be less than one lakh rupees. 
(3) Offences relating to spurious or adulterated drugs to be made non-
bailable and cognizable. 
(4) Provision for setting up of special courts to try offences of spurious 
or adulterated drugs. 
(5) To confer powers upon police officers not below the rank of sub-
inspector or other designated officer to institute prosecutions under the said 
Act. 
The proposed amendments will make the law deterrent to the offenders 
involved in the manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. The involvement of 
enforcing agencies like police will help in  speedy investigations to look the 
culprits and in controlling anti-social elements involved in such activities.

FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) UNAIDS

an indigenous AIDS vaccine that will address the strains of the HIV subtype 'C

the vaccine is likely to undergo priase-l clinical trial in 2005.

Neo-natal screening to detect genetic defects 
1890. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: W ill the Minister of of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that a Delhi based lab has claimed 
that their neo-natal screening will detect genetic defects early and prevent 
irreversible damage; 
(b) if so, whether Government would consider making the same 
available in major Government hospitals in the country; and 
(c) the complete details of such screening? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Yes, Sir. Lai's 
Path Labs, New Delhi has introduced for the first time in India "Tandem Mass 
Spectrometry" for diagnosing genetic and metabolic disorders and for newborn 
screening. 
(b) This equipment is currently not  available at any Government 
hospital in the country. However, a Multi-Centric Task Force on Inborn 
Metabolic Errors and Newborn Screening has been planned to be initiated by 
Indian Council of Medical Research. A Public-Private Partnership involving 
the said Lab in Delhi for earring out the screening for genetic disorders at a 
very subsidised cost under collaborative programme is also being thought 
upon. 
(c) The Newborn screening can enable ear ly detection of inborn errors 
metabolism, which if left undiagnosed and untreated could lead to mental 
retardation, crippling disability, development delay and even death. This 
equipment can detect more than 30 disorder from a single drop of blood and 
more than 500 samples can be tested per day. The screening can help to prevent 
the recurrence of similar births and many of the metabolic disorders can be 
treated with nutritional interventions by diets, many of which are currently 
unavailable in the country.

Committees on Railway Accidents 
1916. SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Will th e Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: . 
(a) whether the recommendations of various Committees including 
Prakash Narain Committee on Railway accidents have since been considered 
and action taken on them; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) and (b) Between 1960 and 1980, three High Powered 
Committees viz. Railway Accidents Committee— 1962 (K unzru Committee), 
Railway Accidents Inquir y Committee— 1968 (Wanchoo Committee) and 
Railway Accidents Enquiry Committee- 1978 (Sikri Committee) went into the 
entire gamut of Railway working and suggested measures for improving the 
Railway Safety. Action for implementation of the accepted recommendations of 
these Committees was taken. 
Thereafter, Railway Safety Review Committee i.e. RSRC (Khanna 
Committee) had been set up in 1998 to, inter alia, review the position of 
accidents on the Indian Railways and to review the implementation of the 
recommendations made by the earlier Committees and to make their own 
recommendations. The Railway Safety Review Committee made a total of 278 
recommendations in both the parts of its report. Of the 242 recommendations, 
which have been accepted fully or partially, 92 have already been 
implemented. Other accepted recommenda tions are at various stages of 
implementation depending upon the availability of resources. 
There was no Prakash Narain Committee on railway accidents. 
However, a National Transportation Safety Board had been set up in 1987 
under the Cabinet Secretariat, with the main objective of bringing about 
improvements in safety in different transport sectors like Railways, Civil 
Aviation, Road Transport etc. This Board was wound up with effect from 1st 
April, 1990. Shri Prakash Narain was the Chairman of National Transportation 
Safety Board. 
After winding up the National Transportation Safety Board, some 
recommendations pertaining to Railways were communicated to the Ministry 
of Railways on which action as warranted was taken.

More Powers to RPF 
1923.       PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Railway Protection Force was provided with more powers 
to deal with crimes on trains and railway premises to make rail travel safe; 
(b) whether measures announced in the railway budget have been 
introduced in the railways for curbing offences like sabotage, damage or 
destruction of railway property and hurting people; and 
(c) if so, the what extent  these measures have helped in checking the 
crimes and robberies? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS: 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) Yes, Sir. Railway Protection Force (RPF) has been 
entrusted with the responsibilities for better protection of passengers and passenger 
area (in addition to Railway Property) by the amendments to the Railway 
Protection ForceAct, 1957 and made responsible for minor offences which affect 
the passengers and the Railway System under chapter XV of the Railway Act, 
1989. RPF has taken up escorting of some trains to supplement efforts of the 
Govt. Railway Police (GRP) and also supplement security in many stations, so 
that the GRP (under the State Government) can better focus on serious crimes. 
The task of escorting of trains is being shared by RPF in*co-ordination with the 
Govt. Railway Police to make rail travel safe. 
(b) and (c) The amendments came in to force with e ffect from 1st of 
July, 2004. RPF has taken up escorting of many trains in co-ordination with GRP 
In July 2004 average of 1,288 trains were escorted daily by RPF. While 
escorting, RPF staff keep vigil and prevent crimes. 
However Sections 150, 151 & 152 of the Railways Act 1989, pertaining 
to sabotage and related wrecking of/damage to trains and Railway Properties 
and causing hurt to people etc. are still in the jurisdiction of the Govt. Railway 
Police (GRP) of the States/Union Territory. The investigation and prosecution 
of crime under the Indian Penal Code as well as sabotage related cases under 
the Railways Act, 1989 continue to be with the State Police. 
206 

[20 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA  
 
 After RPF has started escorting of trains in co-ordination with GRP, 
there has not been any gruesome or sensational case of crime or robbery in the 
train escorted by them. The cases of theft of Luggage, Chain snatching, 
drugging are dealt with promptitude in collaboration with Govt. Railway Police. 
Due to the efforts of RPF, 29 persons for luggage theft and snatching of 
Jewellery and one person for drugging were apprehended. 
The Railways are closely coordinating with the State Governments for 
prevention and detection of cases of violent incidents and take the following 
steps in this regard:— 
(i) Periodical coordination meetings right from the RPF Post-Police 
Station level to the General Manager-Home Secretary level. 
Whenever there is any flare up in the number and nature of incidents, special 
meetings are held for better ground level coordination. 
(ii) RPF has been supplementing th e efforts of the State Government 
Railway Police by deploying additional staff of RPF/RPSF (Railway 
Protection Special Force). 
(iii) RPF has also taken up escorting of trains in crime-effected areas. Such 
crime prone areas have been identified on the basis of reports of 
crime and discussion with State Govt. Police. 
(iv) The Railways has also corresponded with concerned Chief 
Secretaries and Director Generals Police inviting their attention for 
improving the security scenario over the railways. 
(v) Special care has been taken by Railways to provide security to women 
passengers by organizing Women Squads like Surakshini, 
Tejaswani, Durgavahani. Such squads regularly check the women 
compartments to ensure trouble free travel to women passengers. 
(vi) Efforts to institutionalize the sharing of actionable intelligence in crime 
prone States, where the Government Railway Police, RPF officers and 
Intelligence Officers will meet regularly is being pursued. 
All feasible assistance to augm ent the efforts of the State 
administrations in tackling violence in  trains and railway premises is 
extended by the Railways.

Increasing the prices of steel by companies 
†1933. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD.  
              SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the steel producing companies of the country have 
again announced to increase the prices of steel during July and August, 2004; 
(b) if so, the names of companies which have increased the prices of steel and to 
what extent they have increased the prices of steel; 
(c) whether reasons for such increase have also been mentioned; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and whether Government have taken pny measures 
to keep check on such hike? 
THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (c) The 
Government monitors the domestic market prices of steel items but does not maintain price 
data on steel sold by individual steel producing companies. The trend in domestic market 
prices of key steel items prevailing during April, 2004 to August, 2004 in the Mumbai 
market is given belowv—

While there was a general reduction in steel prices during July 2004, the 
prices have increased during August 2004. In case of public sector units, 
Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. (RINL) has not increased the ex-works price since 
13.5.2004. Similarly, SAIL has also not changed the listed ex-works price of 
steel materials since July, 2004. 
(d) The domestic steel prices have generally moved in tandem with the 
international prices. The rise in demand for steel and the increased prices of 
essential raw materials are the main reasons for the price rise. In the domestic 
market the price rise during August, 2004 can be attributed to increase in Excise 
Duty (8% to 12%) and Service tax (8% to 10%) and the imposition of 
Education Cess (2%). 
In a liberalized environment the Government does not intervene 
directly in the market to influence prices. However, the Government, through 
its policy initiatives, has taken various measures to increase availability and 
stabilize the prices, which inter-alia include:— 
(i) Reduction in customs duty on non alloy steel from 25% to 10%. 
(ii) Reduction in customs duty on alloy steel from 25% to 15%. 
(iii) Abolition of 4% Special Additional Duty (SAD) on imports. 
(iv) Lowering of excise duty on steel items from 16% to 12%. 
(v) Lowering customs duty on several raw materials like coal, coke, 
nickel, refractories, pig iron and sponge iron. 
(vi) Substantial increase in the allocation of steel items, during 2004-05, for 
supply to the SSI units under the existing scheme for supply to SSI 
unit. 
(vii) A temporary suspension of DEPB benefits on steel exports from 
27.3.2004 to 12.7.2004.
